It makes sense from a build-as-a-service point of view. That's basically Red Hat's business model - they supply support and a nicely packaged system, and companies pay for their services because it's cheaper than keeping a full inhouse Linux team.

There is no problem with GPL software. As I understand it, early in the days of the FSF (80s-90s), they actually made a few hundred bucks every time someone ordered a tape to be made of the current versions of all of their software.

Most GPL software that is "sold" includes either special add-ons (say, special package management software for a Linux distro), which may be proprietary or offer additional value in other ways (such as online services), or includes support in some manner, which is IIRC the idealized form of making money for an OSS development company.

This ruling does not impact this business model in any negative way. If anything, it enforces its basic legal backing.
